newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Spring says N.Ireland climate difficult.
newsitem.headline: Spring says N.Ireland climate difficult.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said on Thursday that growing support for maverick Protestant Loyalist Billy Wright had complicated the search for a lasting Northern Ireland settlement.

Spring told Irish RTE radio that public backing for Wright marked a continuation of militant Protestant opposition to the peace talks which exploded over the summer in Protestant parades and riots across the province.

"I would see it as an unfortunate continuation of the deterioration of the situation which took place in the summer," Spring said before talks with Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew.

The Combined Loylist Military Command, the umbrella group for Protestant guerrillas fighting to keep Northern Ireland British, gave Wright until midnight last Saturday to leave Northern Ireland for opposing their policies.

On Wednesday night thousands of people attended a rally in support of Wright, who has been convicted of security offences and is said by security sources to be close to the leadership of one faction of outlawed Ulster Volunteer Force guerrillas.

Wright was feted like a hero at the rally and told his supporters he opposed the policies of Loyalist parties taking part in the peace talks because the negotiations were aimed at ending British rule of Northern Ireland.
"I will not become part of a process that is designed to ease our people into a united Ireland, " said Wright. "I am living through the death of our nation and the destruction of our way of life."

He has cast himself as leader of a breakaway faction of Loyalists, so-called because of their allegiance to Britain, and an opponent of two Loyalist parties who want Protestant guerrillas to maintain a 23-month ceasefire.
The Wright affair is expected to dominate Thursday's talks to prepare the ground for the resumption of multi-party Northern Ireland negotiations in Belfast next Monday.
Spring acknowledged that the row had complicated the already fraught peace talks, which have made virtually no headway since they began in June.

"The background is very difficult but notwithstanding that I believe very strongly that there is an obligation on both governments and hopefully the parties to bring momentum to those talks and to avoid further deterioration of the situation," he said.

The British and Irish governments have hinted that two small hard-line parties representing Loyalist militia, the Progressive Unionist Party and Ulster Democratic Party, might be removed from the talks unless the death threat against Wright is lifted.
They have said that all participants in the negotiations have to abide by principles of non-violence and that the threats against Wright are incompatible with democracy.
Sinn Fein, political wing of IRA guerrillas fighting British rule of the province, has been barred from the talks because of the guerrillas' failure to reinstate a ceasefire they broke in February.

The removal of the hard-line Loyalist parties would leave only established mainstream political groups at the talks who have been unable to make any headway towards a Northern Ireland settlement for 27 years.
